lesson.title: Likes, Shares, and Divides: Social Media Remakes American Politics
lesson.summary: Platforms built on the Digital Revolution's internet infrastructure changed how Americans got political information, and researchers continue to debate how much that change deepened political polarization.
lesson.body:
Social media grew directly out of the Digital Revolution's internet infrastructure, but it changed how Americans consumed political information in ways that older technologies, radio, television, and newspapers, never could. Understanding this shift requires looking first at how the platforms developed, and second at the ongoing debate among researchers over how much they actually changed American politics.

The major platforms arrived in a short span of years. Friendster launched in 2002 and MySpace in 2003, but the platform that became dominant was Facebook, founded by Mark Zuckerberg and classmates at Harvard University in 2004 and opened to the general public in 2006. YouTube followed in 2005, Twitter in 2006, and Instagram in 2010. Apple's iPhone, introduced in 2007, and the wave of smartphones that followed put these platforms in people's pockets at all times, not just at a desktop computer. By the early 2010s, a large share of American adults were getting news and political commentary through social media feeds rather than through a small number of national television networks and local newspapers.

What made these feeds different was the algorithm behind them. Rather than showing users a neutral chronological list of posts, platforms increasingly used software to predict which content would keep a person scrolling, clicking, and commenting, and content that provoked strong emotion, including anger and outrage, tended to perform well by that measure. Commentators, including internet activist Eli Pariser in his 2011 book The Filter Bubble, argued that this created echo chambers in which users mostly saw content that confirmed their existing views, reinforced by algorithmic curation rather than a person's deliberate choice.

Social media also gave ordinary users, activists, and political movements a way to organize and reach audiences directly, without needing access to a newspaper editor or a television producer. This was visible internationally during the Arab Spring protests of 2010 and 2011, when platforms like Twitter and Facebook helped coordinate demonstrations across the Middle East and North Africa, and it became visible domestically as movements across the political spectrum used hashtags and viral posts to build support.

Researchers continue to debate how large a causal role social media plays in American political polarization, as opposed to simply reflecting divisions that already existed. Studies have found evidence that algorithmic feeds can deepen the sense of division between political groups and that disinformation spreads efficiently on these platforms, a concern that became especially prominent after revelations in 2018 that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica had harvested Facebook user data to build political advertising profiles. Other researchers caution that polarization was rising in the United States before social media existed and point to other causes, discussed further in the study of political polarization more broadly. What is not in dispute is that social media fundamentally changed the pace, volume, and personalization of political communication in America.
